body:
## Problem

#711 split the cardinality gauges so the exposed total reconciles with a scrape. It does, exactly —
verified live against the <soak-host> soak on 2026-08-12:

```
meraki_exporter_cardinality_product_series  4829
meraki_exporter_cardinality_self_series        6
meraki_exporter_cardinality_exposed_series  4835   # == sample-line count of /metrics
```

The reconciliation is correct and is **not** in question. The naming is.

`_CARDINALITY_SELF_METRIC_NAMES` (`core/cardinality.py:31`) is deliberately narrow — it lists only
the `CardinalityMonitor`'s own seven families, with a comment explaining why the broad
`meraki_exporter_` prefix was rejected. Consequently `self_series` means "series emitted by the
cardinality monitor", while **every other** `meraki_exporter_*` family counts as
`product_series`.

On the same live scrape there are **891** `meraki_exporter_*` sample lines. So `product_series`
= 4829 includes roughly **885 exporter self-instrumentation series** — about **18%** of the number.
An operator reading `product_series` as "how much Meraki product data am I storing" is overstated by
that much, and the drill-down UI inherits the same split.

## Why file it rather than reopen #711

#711's acceptance was reconciliation, and it delivered that. This is a distinct, milder claim about
what the three names communicate, found by live inspection after #711 closed. Severity LOW.

## Scope

Make the exposed split mean what its names say, without breaking the reconciliation guarantee. The
likely shape is three buckets rather than two — product data, exporter self-instrumentation, and
monitor-own — such that they still sum exactly to the scrape total. Retain
`meraki_exporter_total_series` as the compatibility alias it already is, and keep whatever the
existing families report stable or explicitly documented as changed.

The `meraki_exporter_` prefix is the natural discriminator for the self bucket, and the existing code
comment's objection to it must be addressed head-on rather than ignored: if some
`meraki_exporter_*` family genuinely carries product data, name it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The buckets sum exactly to the Prometheus scrape sample count; a test pins it.
- [ ] Exporter self-instrumentation is no longer counted as product data.
- [ ] `/cardinality` and its drill-downs present the same split as the gauges.
- [ ] Generated metrics docs describe precisely what each family counts.
- [ ] Any change in an existing family's meaning is called out in the upgrade notes.

comments.body:
Phase-A implementation checkpoint (uncommitted lane work): added the product/exporter/monitor three-way accounting and a focused reconciliation regression test.

Consumer disposition: no `grafana/**` queries reference `meraki_exporter_cardinality_product_series`, `meraki_exporter_cardinality_exporter_series`, or `meraki_exporter_total_series`; `/status` has no consumer. The cardinality UI is updated in-scope. The integration pass must regenerate generated metrics docs and add the upgrade-note disposition for the changed `product_series` meaning.

Focused pytest and Ruff are green; no Meraki API calls.

body:
## Problem

#695 made the control POSTs fail closed and made the UI disable its buttons when
`server.api_token` is **unset**. It left the opposite case wrong: when a token **is** configured,
`control_api_enabled` is true, so `templates/index.html` renders the buttons **enabled**
(`app.py:969`, `app.py:1090`), but the page's `fetch` sends no `Authorization` header. Every click
returns 401.

There is no security bypass — the server is correct, which is why the wave-1 audit rated this LOW.
The defect is honesty: the UI advertises a control it cannot perform, and it does so specifically in
the configured-token deployments that are the *secure* ones.

`templates/clients.html` has the same shape for the clear-DNS-cache control and must be checked.

## Decision (frozen)

**Hide the control buttons entirely whenever the browser cannot authenticate; controls are
API-only.** Chosen 2026-08-12, extending D1 ("fail closed, no escape hatch; UI hides the buttons")
to the configured-token case.

Explicitly rejected, and not to be re-litigated:

- **A browser unlock field holding the token in JS memory** — puts an operator secret into page
  memory, so any XSS on the page exfiltrates it. Rejected in favour of adding no new exposure.
- **A real login with an HttpOnly cookie plus CSRF** — introduces session lifetime, CSRF handling
  and cookie scoping as a new security surface, for a convenience button. Rejected as
  disproportionate.

## Scope

The UI never renders an enabled control it cannot successfully call. With a token configured the
buttons are absent (not merely `disabled`), with a short inline note pointing at the documented API
invocation. With no token configured, #695's existing disabled-plus-tooltip state is already correct
and stays.

Docs gain the copy-paste authenticated invocation, e.g.:

```
curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $MERAKI_EXPORTER_SERVER__API_TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:9099/api/collectors/trigger
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With `server.api_token` set, `/` renders no enabled trigger button and no button that 401s.
- [ ] With `server.api_token` unset, the existing disabled state and tooltip are unchanged.
- [ ] `/clients` clear-DNS-cache control audited and given the same treatment.
- [ ] A test asserts both rendered states, keyed on token presence.
- [ ] Docs show the authenticated `curl` for every control endpoint.
- [ ] No token value, or any derivative of one, is rendered into HTML or JS in either state.

body:
## Problem

`make check` is the documented local gate (`CLAUDE.md`: "NEVER commit without running linters and
type checks") but it does not check formatting:

```make
check: lint typecheck test
lint:
	uv run ruff check .
```

`ruff check` does not enforce `ruff format`. CI does. So a tree with unformatted files passes the
local gate and fails CI.

## Evidence this is not theoretical

It happened during wave 1. Local `make check` passed at the composed tree; exact-head CI run
`31643397135` then failed on two unformatted fixture files, requiring the formatting-only repair
commit `8383656` and a second CI round-trip. The wave-1 report names this as a false pass.

## Scope

Add `ruff format --check .` to the local gate so it matches CI. Options: fold it into the `lint`
target, or add a `format-check` target and put it in `check`'s prerequisites. Prefer whichever
matches how CI invokes it, so the two cannot drift again.

Then verify the gate actually fails: deliberately unformat a file, run `make check`, quote the
failure, revert.

Also confirm no *other* CI gate is missing locally. CI runs at least `actionlint`, `helm lint`,
`kubeconform`, `git diff --check` and a Docker smoke test. This issue does not require adding all of
them to `make check` — it requires knowing which are absent and saying so, so the difference between
"the local gate" and "the real gate" is documented rather than discovered per incident.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `make check` fails on an unformatted file; the failure output is quoted in the closing comment.
- [ ] `make check` passes on the formatted tree.
- [ ] The set of CI gates NOT covered by `make check` is enumerated in the contributing/dev docs.
- [ ] No change to CI's own behaviour, which was already correct.

body:
## Problem

`core/discovery.py::DiscoveryService.run_discovery()` makes real Meraki SDK calls through raw
`asyncio.to_thread`, bypassing the `MerakiApiFacade` that #698 established as the single paced,
instrumented boundary:

- `discovery.py:74` — `api.organizations.getOrganizations`
- `discovery.py:136` — `api.organizations.getOrganization` (single-org path)
- `discovery.py:143` — `api.organizations.getOrganizations` (multi-org path)
- `discovery.py:169` — `api.organizations.getOrganizationNetworks` (per org, `total_pages="all"`)

#698's AST regression gate (`tests/unit/test_698_api_facade_gate.py`) scopes its scan to
`api/`, `services/`, `collectors/` and `core/api_helpers.py`. `core/discovery.py` is **not** in
`_OWNED_ROOTS`, so these four call sites are invisible to the gate and will stay invisible.

## Why it matters

Three concrete consequences, all of which contradict decisions already frozen in #694:

1. **The attempt counter under-reports.** `meraki_exporter_api_request_attempts_total` and
   `meraki_exporter_api_requests_total` are incremented inside the facade. Discovery's calls never
   reach it, so startup API consumption is invisible. Any capacity or budget arithmetic built on
   those counters (#699, #701) is reading a number it believes is total and is not.
2. **AIMD never sees discovery's throttles.** `OrgRateLimiter.record_throttle_event` is driven from
   the facade. A 429 during discovery is therefore not fed back into the limiter, so the very first
   API traffic the process makes is the one traffic that cannot teach the limiter anything.
3. **Startup is unpaced and scales with org count.** `run_discovery` loops
   `for org in organizations` and issues one paginated `getOrganizationNetworks` per org with no
   token acquisition. On a key with many orgs this is a serial unpaced burst against both the 10 rps
   per-org and 100 rps per-source-IP ceilings documented in #700.

## Scope

Route all four call sites through `MerakiApiFacade.call` using the frozen signature. Discovery
deliberately bypasses `NetworkFilter` for audit purposes and that behaviour must be preserved
exactly — this issue changes *how the call is executed and metered*, not *what it returns* or
*which networks it reports*. The existing `validate_response_format` calls stay.

Then close the gate hole: add `core/discovery.py` to `_OWNED_ROOTS` in
`tests/unit/test_698_api_facade_gate.py` so a future raw call there fails.

Consider whether `api/client.py:199` (`self._api = await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, the SDK
constructor) should be explicitly documented as an intentional non-request exemption rather than
merely not matching the gate's `self.api`-rooted pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four `discovery.py` SDK call sites go through `MerakiApiFacade.call`.
- [ ] Discovery still reports the full pre-filter network inventory; `NetworkFilter` is still
      bypassed there and a test pins that behaviour.
- [ ] `core/discovery.py` is in the #698 gate's `_OWNED_ROOTS`, and the gate is proven to reject a
      deliberately reintroduced raw call in that file (quote the failure).
- [ ] Discovery's calls increment the facade attempt counter; a test asserts the count after a
      simulated multi-org discovery.
- [ ] A 429 raised during discovery reaches `record_throttle_event`.
- [ ] The SDK-constructor call site is either routed or documented as an explicit exemption.

comments.body:
Wave 2 L6 implementation complete; awaiting integration/commit by the root.

- Routed the four discovery SDK calls through `MerakiApiFacade.call`; discovery still intentionally queries the full pre-filter network inventory.
- Extended the #698 AST gate to cover `core/discovery.py`, including API-parameter roots used by `resolve_org_id`.
- Proved the gate negatively by temporarily restoring `asyncio.to_thread(api.organizations.getOrganizations)`: `AssertionError: ['core/discovery.py:78'] == []`; reverted the provocation.
- Focused tests: `16 passed`.

The optional shared limiter argument is ready; L1 will wire the existing manager limiter from `app.py`.

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D18** · Closes finding **F-L7-07** (INFO — measurement, no defect)

## Measurement
An exhaustive closed-set scan counted the files a new thing forces you to edit: **3** for a new
top-level collector, **6** for a fully scheduled device family, excluding generated docs and new tests.
The six seams are separate closed enumerations:

- `core/constants/device_constants.py:9-42` — family enum and product strings
- `collectors/devices/__init__.py:3-20` — public import
- `collectors/device.py:32-44` — parent routing
- `core/scheduler.py:66-220` — endpoint group and shape
- `services/inventory.py:1156-1235` — inventory classification
- `core/constants/metrics_constants.py` — metric enum

## Decision D18
Six seams applies to a genuinely new Meraki **product type**. A new **model subtype of an existing
product costs nothing structural** — Catalyst/CS already routes through the MS collector, and Catalyst
CW through MR, which is the evidence. Six explicit files is manageable and arguably less magical than
declarative registration for something as significant as a new product family.

**No code change required.** This exists so the number is recorded and a future contributor does not
rediscover it, and so any future proposal to add declarative family registration starts from a measured
baseline rather than a feeling.

## Acceptance
- [x] `docs/extending-collectors.md` names the six seams with current `file:line` refs and the 3-versus-6 distinction
- [x] The product-type versus model-subtype distinction from D18 is stated
- [x] Close as documented; no behaviour change

comments.body: Documented in docs/extending-collectors.md: measured three-existing-file cost for a new top-level collector; six named current seams with file:line references for a new product family; D18 distinction that a model subtype costs zero structural seams, evidenced by Catalyst/CS through MS and Catalyst CW through MR. No behavior change.

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D14** · Closes finding **F-L8-06**

## Mechanism
Verified live: the `main` ruleset requires **exactly one** check — `ci-success`
(`.github/workflows/ci.yml:299`). CodeQL, Docker Security, Scorecard, zizmor and dependency-review all
run independently and gate nothing. The reusable publication workflow pushes, signs and attests the
image **before** a non-gating Trivy SARIF scan (`release-please.yml:71-89`, `publish.yml:31`,
`docker-security.yml`). So known-vulnerable code can merge and a known-vulnerable image can ship, then
be signed and attested.

Existing strengths to preserve: all 35 external Actions are pinned to immutable SHAs, images are signed
with SBOMs and SARIF is uploaded. The gap is enforcement, not detection.

The reason detection alone is not enough here is already proven in this repo: CI was red for 20
consecutive runs over two days and nobody noticed.

## Why split by determinism (D14)
A change-scoped scanner failing is always the author's fault and always fixable, so gating it never
blocks on the outside world. Gating everything on merge would stall the repo on third-party CVE
disclosures and, on a solo-maintainer repo, predictably ends with the gate bypassed — which is worse
than not having it.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **Merge** requires `zizmor`, `actionlint` and `dependency-review` alongside `ci-success`
- [ ] **Publication** blocks on HIGH/CRITICAL from Trivy and CodeQL, with **the scan moved before push, sign and attest**
- [ ] A committed exception file carries, per accepted CVE: identifier, reason, and an **expiry date**, so an acceptance resurfaces rather than becoming permanent
- [ ] An expired exception fails the publish gate
- [ ] Signing, SBOM and SARIF upload are all preserved
- [ ] `.whitesource`, `.safety-project.ini` and `.codacy.yaml` are each confirmed to be running or deleted as vestigial
- [ ] Codecov and Codacy uploads are confirmed either required or explicitly best-effort — currently they are token-gated and silently no-op
- [ ] `docs/security.md` documents the gate and the exception policy

comments.body: Wave 2 parking checkpoint: the local merge-gate experiment was reverted because publication ordering lives in the shared rknightion/.github reusable container-publish workflow, outside this repository worktree and the authorised file territory. Wiring only local scanner jobs could falsely report success while publish/sign/attest still precede the blocking scan. This issue remains open with no workflow diff. Resume boundary: update the shared reusable publication workflow so HIGH/CRITICAL Trivy and CodeQL checks run before push/sign/attest, add the expiring exception policy, then wire and prove the consuming workflow here.

## 2026-08-14 authority checkpoint - design complete, shared mutation still unauthorised

Live ruleset 6568364 still requires only `ci-success`; the exact additional contexts are `actionlint / Run actionlint`, `zizmor / Run zizmor`, and `dependency-review / Dependency review`. Publication still pushes architectures and manifest, signs, attests, and emits SBOM before non-gating Trivy; independent CodeQL has no publication dependency.

Read-only discovery found shared remote main `f75c257695aee3e83ecc9bbf94bcdf2117cf307b` while the sibling checkout is stale; latest release is v1.6.1 and open Release Please PR #49 proposes v1.6.2. The gating feature must be released first and consumers pinned to that actual release SHA. `.whitesource` and `.safety-project.ini` are vestigial; `.codacy.yaml` is active. Codacy coverage executes mutable `master/get.sh` and should be removed while retaining Codacy Cloud static analysis; Codecov should be explicit best-effort. CodeQL needs a SARIF severity evaluator, and exception policy must require reason and expiry.

Exact sequence: authorise shared repo/release/ruleset/negative proofs; fast-forward shared checkout; file a shared issue; implement and prove pre-publication gates; release; pin every local shared reference to the immutable release SHA; update the ruleset; complete local policy/docs; verify real publication ordering. No shared, ruleset, release, branch, or negative-run mutation was performed.

2026-08-14 resume audit (read-only): the issue remains valid and the cross-repository boundary is now exact. Exporter ruleset `6568364` still requires only `ci-success`; the additional observed check contexts are `actionlint / Run actionlint`, `zizmor / Run zizmor`, and `dependency-review / Dependency review`.

Publication is still ordered unsafely in the shared `rknightion/.github` reusable: per-architecture image pushes and manifest push happen before signing/attestation/SBOM, and the non-gating Trivy SARIF scan runs only afterward. Independent CodeQL has no dependency edge into publication. The local sibling checkout is stale; remote shared `main` is `f75c257695aee3e83ecc9bbf94bcdf2117cf307b` with green exact-head CI, latest release v1.6.1, and an open v1.6.2 release-please PR.

The required sequence is atomic: implement and test policy/SARIF gates in the shared repo; release them; pin every exporter shared-workflow reference to that released immutable SHA/version; add the expiring exception file and local wiring/docs; then update ruleset 6568364 and prove scan-before-push ordering. Local partial wiring remains deliberately absent.

Still required from Rob before implementation: explicit authority to edit/commit/push/release `rknightion/.github`, update exporter ruleset 6568364, and run controlled negative workflow proofs. No repository or ruleset state was changed by this audit.

Parent: #694 · Closes findings **F-L9-01**, **F-L9-02**, **F-L9-03**, **F-L9-04**, **F-L7-04**, **F-L7-05**

Six documentation defects, each verified against code. Grouped because they land as one docs pass.

## F-L9-01 — README and FAQ promise multi-org polling that startup rejects
`README.md:221` and `docs/faq.md:44-47` say an unset `ORG_ID` monitors all visible organizations.
`core/discovery.py:91-112` **raises** when two or more are visible and requires one instance per org.
The generated config and scaling docs already state the correct single-org contract, so the repo
contradicts itself.

## F-L7-04 — the chart says the same wrong thing
Chart `values.yaml:122-133` comments that an empty organization ID polls every accessible org. Same
correction, separate customer-facing surface, so it needs its own fix.

## F-L9-02 — Helm and deployment docs use a variable the app does not read
`docs/deployment-operations.md:89-106` and chart `CLAUDE.md:81` use `WEBHOOKS__SECRET`. The Pydantic
field is `shared_secret` (`core/config_models.py:808-815`), so the variable is
`WEBHOOKS__SHARED_SECRET`. Anyone following the examples gets a webhook setup that silently fails
authentication until they diagnose it. `.env.example` and the security docs already use the right name.

## F-L9-03 — the scaling guide's network-health arithmetic is obsolete
`docs/scaling-guide.md:72-95` and `:121-141` treat eight groups as per-wireless-network on a 300 s
cadence and describe a simultaneous 3,200-call sweep. Current groups have distinct floors and channel
utilization is org-wide and paginated (`collectors/network_health.py:75-126`). The correct equivalent
gives 4.58 calls/300 s at HOMELAB and about 1,041.3/300 s at `W=400, A=4000` — not 3,200. Operators
making capacity decisions from this are disabling collectors they do not need to, or drawing an
unsupported timeout conclusion. Correcting it does **not** make total LARGE demand sustainable; see
#701.

## F-L9-04 — generated endpoint reference omits auth and side effects
`scripts/generate_endpoints_docs.py:12-18`, `:98-114` — hand-maintained `ENDPOINT_NOTES` covers only
client and webhook enablement, leaving the control trigger, status, config and cardinality routes with
blank notes (`docs/reference/endpoints.md:7-22`). So a **state-changing forced-collection POST**
(`app.py:1102-1168`) reads as an inert route. Coordinate with #695, which changes those routes' auth.

## F-L7-05 — operations docs state the wrong default log format
`docs/deployment-operations.md:253-307` says the default is logfmt and gives `| logfmt` LogQL. The
model default is `json` (`core/config_models.py:1174-1217`, `core/logging.py:18-36`), so copied field
filters fail during exactly the incident someone is trying to diagnose.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L9-01** — README and FAQ state the single-org contract and point at the sharding recipe
- [x] **F-L7-04** — the chart comment is corrected and links the sharding recipe
- [x] **F-L9-02** — every example uses `WEBHOOKS__SHARED_SECRET`, plus a test asserting documented example variables map to real settings fields
- [x] **F-L9-03** — capacity arithmetic is generated from the endpoint groups rather than hand-written, and distinguishes steady-state rate from a due sweep
- [x] **F-L9-04** — every non-trivial route has an explicit note covering auth and side effects, with a generator assertion that no route ships a blank note
- [x] **F-L7-05** — JSON-first examples, with logfmt as a clearly separate opt-in section
- [x] `make docgen` + `make check` green

comments.body: Docs-only corrections complete: README.md and docs/faq.md now describe the single-org startup contract and link sharding; docs/deployment-operations.md and docs/troubleshooting.md are JSON-default with distinct opt-in logfmt examples. The chart values comment, generated capacity arithmetic, generated endpoint notes/assertion, documented-variable test, and final docgen/check gate remain intentionally unchecked for their owners.

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D17** · Closes findings **F-L9-06**, **F-L9-05**

## Mechanism — F-L9-06
`scripts/generate_metrics_docs.py:21-28` still excludes `CircuitBreaker` ("Not wired in") and all of
`async_utils.py` ("CircuitBreaker metrics are not wired in"). **`rg CircuitBreaker src/ tests/`
returns zero hits** — the class does not exist anywhere, and `async_utils.py` defines no metrics at
all. So a whole source file is excluded from metric-doc generation for a reason that evaporated, and
any metric added there in future would be silently undocumented.

Parse errors print and continue (`:446-468`), so a reproducible run can produce **incomplete output
that looks complete**.

Related and the same class of bug: `generate_config_docs.py` walks a **hardcoded `nested_models`
list**, while `generate_env_example.py` walks the settings tree. A new `*Settings` model therefore
appears in `.env.example` and never in `config.md`. `scripts/CLAUDE.md` tells contributors to eyeball
the printed "Found N…" counts — a human check for a machine problem.

## Mechanism — F-L9-05
`scripts/CLAUDE.md:6` states there is no CI check that fails on generated-docs drift.
**That is false** — `.github/workflows/ci.yml:61-72` runs docgen and diffs, and it was red for 20
consecutive runs (2026-08-10 → 2026-08-12) before `ce03473` fixed it. Durable misinformation about a
required gate, aimed squarely at future contributors and agents.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L9-06** — a parse failure exits non-zero
- [x] The dead `CircuitBreaker` and `async_utils.py` exclusions are deleted
- [x] The "Found N…" counts become **assertions** — a generator that finds zero of something it should always find fails
- [x] A check fails when `config.md`'s `nested_models` list diverges from the settings tree `.env.example` walks
- [x] **F-L9-05** — `scripts/CLAUDE.md` describes the CI drift gate accurately
- [x] `make docgen` + `make check` green

comments.body:
Progress (L7, uncommitted shared-worktree implementation):

Implemented the five bounded generator/documentation acceptance items:
- `generate_metrics_docs.py` now raises on any source parse failure, rejects zero discovered metrics, and no longer excludes `CircuitBreaker` or `async_utils.py`.
- `generate_collector_docs.py` now raises on parse failure and rejects zero discovered collectors.
- `generate_config_docs.py` validates its explicit section list against the top-level `Settings` model used by `.env.example`; a missing or unexpected model fails generation.
- `scripts/CLAUDE.md` now documents CI docgen-and-diff enforcement and the machine-checked config-section contract.

Focused regression proof (observed): `uv run pytest tests/unit/test_doc_generators_719.py -q` -> `5 passed in 0.51s`; Ruff and format checks passed for the changed scripts/test; `uv run mypy scripts/generate_metrics_docs.py` -> `Success: no issues found in 1 source file`. A disposable-copy run of all six generators succeeded (353 metrics, 49 collectors), without touching shared generated outputs.

Known scoped limitation: `uv run mypy scripts/generate_metrics_docs.py scripts/generate_collector_docs.py tests/unit/test_doc_generators_719.py` surfaces existing mypy errors in `generate_collector_docs.py`, `generate_config_docs.py`, and imported `generate_env_example.py` (12 errors), outside this issue change; none are newly introduced by the focused metrics check.

Root resume point: run `make docgen` in the real worktree, review/stage any generated artifacts alongside all wave changes, then run the final `make check`. Those two acceptance boxes intentionally remain unchecked.

body:
Parent: #694 · Closes **ANOM-1**. **Blocked by #713.**

## The contradiction
Read from the current tree, three facts:

1. Collector duration is observed **exactly once** per successful `collect()` — `core/collector.py:195-201`, labelled by class name.
2. `run_collector_once` **skips** when the per-collector lock is held — `collectors/manager.py:711` tests `collector_lock.locked()` and returns, so two runs of the same collector should not execute concurrently.
3. `start_time` is set inside `collect()`, after the lock is acquired, so duration should exclude lock and semaphore wait.

The observed soak values contradict all three together. Over a container uptime of ~55,200 s,
`DeviceCollector` recorded `duration_seconds_count = 1,560` and
`duration_seconds_sum = 108,468.71` — a mean of 69.5 s and a **total of 108,468 s of execution inside
a 55,200 s window**. That is a 1.96× oversubscription, which is impossible if runs genuinely serialise
and duration genuinely excludes waiting.

The audit filed this as "unexplained provenance" and stopped. It is stronger than that: **one of the
three facts above is false**, and each candidate is its own bug —

- more than one observation per logical run (double-counting, or sub-collectors sharing the label);
- the lock does not actually serialise (note `manager.py:711` checks `locked()` *before* awaiting the semaphore, so admission is racy — the same non-atomicity as F-L8-01);
- duration includes queue or semaphore wait after all.

## Why it needs a harness
Source reading has reached a dead end, and the original 15-hour container no longer exists — a push to
`main` rebuilt `:main` and watchtower replaced it at `2026-08-12T14:20:09Z` before the audit's first
snapshot. Only an isolated, instrumented process settles it.

Related and possibly the same root: `ClientsCollector` recorded **108,790** observations to
`DeviceCollector`'s 1,560. #703 explains the 1 s wake loop, which accounts for the order of magnitude,
but the audit noted a residual ~2× discrepancy it could not explain.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Which of the three facts is false, established by observation on #713's instance, not by argument
- [ ] The underlying defect fixed, or recorded as correct-with-a-misleading-metric-name and the metric renamed or re-documented
- [ ] `rate(duration_sum)/rate(duration_count)` yields a mean an operator can trust for capacity work, or the metric stops implying that it does
- [ ] The residual `ClientsCollector` ~2× discrepancy is explained or shown to be the same cause
- [ ] A regression test pins whatever the correct observation count per run turns out to be
- [ ] `make check` green

Client scheduling also changed since the historical sample. `time.time()` remains a source risk, but the run contract forbids naming it as the cause without observation.

No regression test or metric rename was manufactured. #713 must retain raw duration count/sum deltas, manager admission/start/end/skip events, request timing, monotonic process timing, and status. Client reconciliation also needs real client-route captures, which are absent.

Resume after #713: run the observation, then either close this as a disproven historical premise or write the failing regression test for the one cause actually observed.

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D10** · Closes findings **F-L7-03**, **F-L7-06**

## Mechanism — F-L7-03
`collectors/manager.py:503-540` and `:623-656` raise on zero resolved networks, but
`app.py:525-576` `_startup_collections` catches **every** exception and starts the loops anyway,
logging "continuing with tiered loops" — directly contradicting the fail-fast promise in
`docs/scaling-guide.md:208-213`. So an include/exclude typo matching zero networks produces a running,
apparently-healthy exporter serving a scoped-away fleet.

**The nuance that makes this subtle:** continuing past a startup exception is **correct** for a
transient Meraki outage and **wrong** for a deterministic config error. The blanket catch cannot tell
them apart, and that inability is the bug.

## Mechanism — F-L7-06
Independently-valid field bounds in `core/config_models.py` permit `collector_timeout` below
`per_fetch_deadline_seconds`, an executor under-provisioned against
`max_concurrent_collectors × concurrency_limit`, and an enabled-collectors list excluding every
registered collector. `collectors/manager.py:365-400` validates unknown names but not an empty
effective set or any cross-field timing contract. Result: deterministic timeouts, or a healthy-looking
empty exporter.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Startup exceptions are **classified** into deterministic-config versus transient-API, and only the transient kind is swallowed
- [ ] **Refuse to start:** zero-match NetworkFilter; empty effective collector set; `collector_timeout` < `per_fetch_deadline_seconds`
- [ ] **Warn loudly and run:** executor under-provisioned against admission; workable-but-unusual pacing
- [ ] A misclassification cannot crash-loop on a transient Meraki failure — test with #713's proxy returning 500s at startup
- [ ] Each refusal path has a unit test and an actionable message naming the offending setting and a fix
- [ ] `docs/scaling-guide.md` fail-fast text matches the implemented behaviour
- [ ] `docs/upgrading.md` notes the new refusals, in case a deployment is unknowingly in one of these states
- [ ] `make docgen` + `make check` green

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D13** · Closes finding **F-L8-04**

## Mechanism
`models/webhook.py:57-86` shows the payload carries `sentAt`, `occurredAt` and `alertId`, but
`core/webhook_handler.py:324-454` checks only schema and shared secret and keeps **no replay cache**.
Any captured valid body can be replayed indefinitely; each replay increments metrics and reapplies
device-down state. Reachable only with webhooks enabled (opt-in). #561 covers other webhook hardening,
not this.

The complication D13 resolves: **Meraki legitimately retries deliveries**, so naive dedupe would hide
real retry behaviour. Splitting the metrics is what lets both be true.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L8-04** — payloads whose `sentAt` falls outside a bounded, configurable window are rejected
- [x] The window has a sane floor for clock skew, and a rejection logs clearly enough to diagnose skew rather than looking like an attack
- [x] A **bounded** TTL cache keyed on `alertId` or a body fingerprint; device state is applied **once per alert**
- [x] `delivery_attempts_total` and `unique_alerts_total` are **separate** metrics, so legitimate retries stay visible while state transitions stay idempotent
- [x] Documented: the cache is per-process, so two replicas each apply state once
- [ ] Replay test **against #713's harness**: the same body twice produces two attempts and one state application
- [x] Payload size is bounded and the body is authenticated before being parsed
- [x] `make docgen` + `make check` green

comments.body:

Implemented at seam `d737893` (uncommitted):

- `WebhookHandler` rejects authenticated deliveries whose `sentAt` is outside `freshness_window_seconds` in either direction, increments `meraki_webhook_stale_rejected_total`, and logs clock-skew guidance.
- A per-process, bounded monotonic-TTL `OrderedDict` caches SHA-256 identities from `alertId`, falling back to a canonical body fingerprint. It evicts expired entries and the oldest entry beyond `replay_cache_max_entries`.
- `meraki_webhook_delivery_attempts_total`, `_unique_alerts_total`, `_replays_rejected_total`, and `_stale_rejected_total` are separately emitted with the frozen `WebhookMetricName` members. A retry remains visible as a delivery while state application is idempotent.

## Mechanism — F-L3-03
`app.py:466-509` shuts the executor down with `wait=False, cancel_futures=True`, never closes the SDK's
`httpx.Client` (`api/client.py:293-302` — the session owns a close method the exporter does not call),
and never shuts down the private DNS pool (`services/dns_resolver.py:57-65`). Cancelling awaits cannot
stop running blocking calls. Helm sends SIGKILL after 150 s (chart `values.yaml:45-59`). So a SIGTERM
during slow SDK or DNS work risks forced termination with lost final work and telemetry during every
rollout or drain. `NOT OBSERVED` in the audit because <soak-host> was deliberately not disturbed — which is
what #713 is for.

Chart `values.yaml:46-59` and `:214-215` permit a **600 s** fetch deadline while
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` stays **150 s** (`templates/deployment.yaml:42`), with no cross-field
validation (`templates/_validation.tpl:1-24`). The chart comments state the rule manually; the
validation omits it, so an avoidable SIGKILL is one override away.

- [ ] **F-L3-03** — shutdown explicitly and boundedly awaits: SDK session close, both executors, and the DNS pool
- [ ] A SIGTERM test **against #713's disposable instance with genuinely blocked SDK threads** shows a clean exit inside the grace period, or a documented bounded worst case
- [ ] **F-L7-02** — chart validation derives or enforces `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` >= fetch deadline + margin

The audit could not induce a single failure mode: it was forbidden from disturbing the live soak, and
a live org cannot produce most of them anyway. You cannot revoke a working key to test revocation, but
a proxy returns 401 all day.

A throwaway containerised exporter against a **recorded Meraki response corpus**, with a proxy in
front that injects, on demand: 429 with varying `Retry-After`, request timeouts, TLS failures and
interception, HTML bodies (captive portal), slow responses, connection resets, 401/403 (revoked key),
and DNS failure.

`<watchtower-container>`, which is what destroyed the audit's 15-hour soak counters when a push
to `main` rebuilt the image.

- [x] Recorded corpus committed, with **every response shape sourced from a real capture, never invented** — per F-L9-08, a corpus that encodes the same wrong assumption as the code proves nothing
- [x] Corpus entries state their capture date and the family they came from; absent families are marked `SHAPE-ASSUMED` and cannot be presented as verified
- [x] Proxy supports every injection mode listed above, selectable per test

## Mechanism — F-L7-01
`charts/meraki-dashboard-exporter/values.yaml:358-383` always renders 256Mi request / 512Mi limit
regardless of fleet size. The chart's own comments call 512Mi SMALL-only and say it **will OOMKill at

## Mechanism — F-L4-01
About **74 live series per observed switch port** (`collectors/devices/ms.py:85`), with no default
port-family profile, and `generate_latest(REGI<net-name-6>Y)` (`app.py:992-1008`) serialising the whole registry
on one of two serving threads. Measured: 2,225 `meraki_ms_*` samples over 30 ports; 4,627 samples /
738,423 bytes rendered in 0.223904 s. Projections — MEDIUM ~215k, LARGE ~2.1m, XL ~9.5m series, with
LARGE wire/time around 335 MB / 102 s if rendering stays linear. The chart and docs say 0.6–1.1m for
LARGE, from stale evidence. **Both figures rest on assumed fleet mixes**, which is precisely what
#707 replaces.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L7-01** — shipped defaults cover a measured MEDIUM fleet, with the source measurement cited in the values comment
- [ ] LARGE guidance kept in `docs/scaling-guide.md` and the chart comments, and made consistent with the measurement
- [ ] **F-L4-01** — the LARGE series projection is replaced by a measured `DENSE-SWITCH` figure, and the stale 0.6–1.1m estimate is corrected everywhere it appears
- [ ] Scrape render time and payload size measured at `DENSE-SWITCH`, and checked against a typical Prometheus scrape timeout and the two-thread serving executor

## Live measurement anchor: real RSS for a HOMELAB-shaped fleet

This issue asks for Helm defaults sized from a measured fleet. Here is the one real measurement
available, so the extrapolation starts from evidence rather than from the current defaults.

**Peak RSS over 14 days**, <soak-host> soak via the m7kni stack, 2026-08-12:

```promql
max_over_time(process_resident_memory_bytes{job=~".*meraki.*"}[14d])
# 137,756,672  (131 MiB)   job="meraki-dashboard-exporter"
# 136,036,352  (130 MiB)   job="meraki-dashboard-exporter"
# 155,385,856  (148 MiB)   job="meraki_dashboard"
```

**Series at that RSS**, from a direct scrape of `<soak-host>:9099/metrics` the same day:

```
meraki_exporter_cardinality_exposed_series  4835
  of which product_series 4829, monitor self_series 6
sample lines in /metrics                    4835   (reconciles exactly)
```

So: **~148 MiB peak at ~4.8k series, one network, HOMELAB shape.**

Current defaults for comparison (`charts/meraki-dashboard-exporter/values.yaml:387`):

```yaml
requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi}
limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
```

HOMELAB therefore peaks at about **58% of the 256Mi request** and **29% of the 512Mi limit**. The
defaults are not wrong for the smallest shape — which means the case for changing them has to be
made from a MEDIUM measurement, not from this anchor. Use this only to calibrate the fixture-driven
projection and to sanity-check it: a projection that cannot reproduce ~148 MiB at 4.8k series is
mis-calibrated and must not be used to move a default.

Two cautions:

- **The counter/gauge history restarts on every push to `main`** (watchtower redeploys the soak), so
  this is a peak over several process lifetimes, not one continuous 14-day run.
- **RSS is not linear in series count.** Python heap growth, the client store, the DNS cache and the
  inventory cache each scale on their own dimension, so do not project MEDIUM by multiplying
  148 MiB by a series ratio. Measure with the #707 presets and report which component grew.

Wave 2 measurement checkpoint: the authorised live anchor remains 148.19 MiB RSS at 4,835 exposed series. The local HOMELAB fixture measured about 90.45 MiB and only 125 benchmark series, so it failed the required calibration check and cannot justify changing the Helm request/limit. No values.yaml change was made and this issue remains open. Resume boundary: build a calibrated runtime benchmark that reproduces the HOMELAB anchor, then measure at least one MEDIUM preset and apply D11 from that measured RSS.

## 2026-08-14 measurement checkpoint - still parked behind #713 and a MEDIUM decision

The Wave 2 benchmark remains non-load-bearing: it populated selected caches and a synthetic 125-series registry rather than the exporter, and its HOMELAB RSS was 38.96% below the authorised 148.19 MiB / 4,835-series anchor.

The full-runtime design is now frozen: fresh process per preset, real `ExporterApp`/registry/caches/collectors, strict replay coverage, external RSS sampling through collection/cardinality/scrapes, actual HTTP payload/render timing, and two concurrent scrapes. Predeclared HOMELAB calibration is series within +/-5%, max RSS within +/-15% on the same host/container class, exact topology/cache counts, and zero unmatched routes.

Two blockers remain: #713 has no provenance-bearing corpus, and BRANCH-RETAIL is not MEDIUM. Durable docs define MEDIUM as about 50 networks / 1,000 devices; BRANCH-RETAIL is 750 networks / 4,500 devices and its MX rows are SHAPE-ASSUMED. No Helm default changed.

Resume after #713 by freezing a literal MEDIUM family/port/SSID/client mix, adding the missing fixture `productType` contract, then measuring HOMELAB, MEDIUM, and DENSE-SWITCH. Only measured results may change sizing or scrape guidance.

2026-08-14 measurement design checkpoint: the Wave 2 component benchmark remains unusable for sizing. A valid replacement must launch the real `ExporterApp` in a fresh process, execute the real collector/registry/cache paths against #713's strict captured corpus, scrape the real HTTP `/metrics` path, and sample RSS through collection, cardinality analysis, and concurrent scrape rendering.

Two stale assumptions are now explicit. BRANCH-RETAIL (750 networks / 4,500 devices) is not the documented MEDIUM class (roughly 50 networks / 1,000 devices), so it will not be silently relabelled. The existing fixture also omits device `productType`, which makes scheduler shape accounting incomplete. No Helm default will change until a literal MEDIUM family/port/client mix is frozen and measured. DENSE-SWITCH likewise needs real captured MS response coverage before its 96,000 ports can be load-bearing evidence.

Resume dependency: #713 first supplies the strict replay/provenance seam and complete enough real HOMELAB shapes; then calibration must land within predeclared series/RSS tolerances against the 4,835-series / 148.19 MiB anchor before MEDIUM or DENSE-SWITCH measurements can justify chart/docs changes. `values.yaml` remains unchanged.

## 2026-08-14 post-harness sizing reassessment

#713 and #714 are now complete, but the evidence boundary is narrower than the earlier
"blocked behind #713" wording implied. The committed replay corpus contains exactly four
LIVE-VERIFIED operations: `getOrganization`, `getOrganizationNetworks`,
`getOrganizationDevices`, and `getOrganizationDevicesAvailabilities`. That is enough for failure,
duration, and shutdown proofs, but not for a full production collector/runtime sizing run.

The current harness cannot populate the complete registry, collector surface, caches, or product
routes needed to reconcile HOMELAB against the authorised 4,835-series / 148.19 MiB anchor.
`FleetFixture.measured_report()` still measures a supplied synthetic registry rather than the real
`ExporterApp` HTTP `/metrics` render path.

MEDIUM remains undefined as a concrete fixture. Durable scaling docs describe roughly 50 networks /
1,000 devices; BRANCH-RETAIL is 750 networks / about 4,500 devices and is not being relabelled.
DENSE-SWITCH remains synthetic and lacks LIVE-VERIFIED MS port-status, usage, packet, PoE, stack,
and related routes, so a 96,000-port RSS/payload/render result cannot yet be load-bearing.

No Helm memory default changed. Exact missing evidence:

1. bounded read-only corpus expansion for the full HOMELAB MR/MS/MT collector routes;
2. a full-runtime benchmark around real `ExporterApp`, collectors, registry, caches, RSS sampling,
   cardinality analysis, HTTP render timing, and two concurrent scrapes;
3. HOMELAB calibration against 4,835 series and 148.19 MiB within the frozen tolerances;
4. a documented literal MEDIUM family/port/SSID/client mix;
5. complete LIVE-VERIFIED MS corpus coverage before DENSE-SWITCH measurement.

Resume with the bounded HOMELAB corpus expansion, calibrate HOMELAB first, then measure literal
MEDIUM and DENSE-SWITCH. Until then D11 forbids replacing the current 256Mi/512Mi defaults with
another unsupported number.

body:
Parent: #694 · Closes findings **F-L3-01**, **F-L3-04**

## Mechanism — F-L3-01
`core/async_utils.py:246-317` creates the task at `:293` and acquires the semaphore at `:353`, so
`asyncio.create_task` runs **before** the task enters the bound — all N task, coroutine and context
objects exist while only five execute. Across 14 production call sites. Default MR signal quality
gives `T = D_MR` (up to 5,000 tasks at LARGE); optional Insight gives `T = N × min(A, 30)` (up to
15,000). The advertised cap is real for execution and not for allocation. Partially covered by
closed #248.

## Mechanism — F-L3-04
`collectors/manager.py:89-92` admits 5 collectors × 5 fan-out = **25 logical SDK calls against 10
executor workers** (`api/client.py:61-76`, `app.py:407-412`), so `Q = max(25 - 10, 0) = 15` wait for a
thread. The outer deadline (`core/error_handling.py:454-486`) **includes invisible executor queue
time** and emits only `TIMEOUT`. A request that spent its whole deadline queued for a thread has been
starved, not slowed — and the two are indistinguishable in the metrics, so an operator misdiagnoses
local starvation as Meraki latency and may worsen it by raising retries or deadlines.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L3-01** — producer back-pressure or a worker queue, so in-flight allocation tracks the concurrency bound rather than the fan-out size
- [x] Pending-task metrics exported
- [x] **F-L3-04** — either align admission (`max_concurrent_collectors × concurrency_limit`) with `executor_workers`, or export active/queued/wait-phase so the distinction is visible
- [x] Expiry caused **before execution began** is classified distinctly from a slow upstream response
- [x] Assert allocation and queue behaviour against the `CAMPUS` and `DENSE-SWITCH` presets
- [x] `make check` green

comments.body: Shipped on `main` in `9e975040e87b1582467a3444351139de7855154d`. Producer admission now applies back-pressure before task allocation; outer collector admission is aligned to the SDK executor; pending, active, queue-wait, and pre-start-expiry metrics are emitted; and pre-start expiry is distinct from active execution timeout. CAMPUS and DENSE-SWITCH allocation tests pass. The composed final gate passed Ruff, formatter, mypy over 121 source files, and 2,684 tests.

## Mechanism — F-L3-02
`services/dns_resolver.py:291-401` passes **every** lookup to `asyncio.gather` at `:363` before the
internal five-way semaphore, so with clients enabled up to **25,000 task and future objects exist
while only five run**. Cancelling the waits cannot interrupt running `gethostbyaddr` threads. Caps are
10,000/network and 25,000 total (`collectors/clients.py:603-616`,
`core/config_models.py:961-975`). No queue-depth metric exists.

Every admitted client IP goes to `socket.gethostbyaddr` (`services/dns_resolver.py:264-315`)
unconditionally when clients are enabled. The upstream recipient depends on the host resolver, and
DEBUG logs the IP and hostname. `docs/privacy.md:24-84` describes the cache and the result but **not
the query destination**, and there is no opt-out independent of client collection.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L3-02** — a bounded work queue replaces the whole-cap `gather`; in-flight allocation is proportional to the concurrency limit, not the client cap
- [ ] Queue depth, wait time and timeout metrics are exported

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D2** · Closes findings **F-L9-07**, **F-L9-08**

The keystone of P3. **Blocks the Helm resource default (#712)**, which must take its number from the
`MEDIUM`-class preset's measured RSS rather than a judgement call.

## Why
Three audit lanes each invented their own LARGE fleet and got three different answers — 14.99 rps,
9.02 rps and ~2.1m series — so nothing was falsifiable. Two structural facts make the invented mixes
wrong as well as inconsistent: Meraki caps **MX at 2 and MG at 4 per network**, making "1,000 devices
per family bucket, evenly distributed" impossible; and real published estates are **branch-shaped**
(SPAR ICS 3,500 stores, Visionworks 740 locations, a 500-store retailer, community operators with
1,000+ networks in one org), which no lane modelled despite most of this exporter's cost scaling with
network count.

**F-L9-08:** no test executes a many-network collector + inventory + SDK/executor path. Existing mocks
invent and normalise shapes (`tests/helpers/mock_api.py:343-500`) and representative tests assert cost
existence or dummy concurrency (`tests/unit/test_device_scheduler_gates.py:114-140`,
`test_collector_base.py:205-222`, `test_nh_gate_semantics_629.py:150-171`,
`test_golden_metrics_exposition.py:228-235`).

**F-L9-07:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml:267-304` runs `pytest -m slow` weekly; **no test carries the
marker**, so pytest exits 5 and the workflow rewrites 5 to success. A scheduled CI job that
structurally cannot fail. This work is its real payload.

## Design
One generator parameterised by `(networks, per-family device counts, ports/switch, SSIDs/network,
clients)`. Seven presets:

| Preset | Shape | Stresses |
|---|---|---|
| `HOMELAB` | 1 net / 19 dev (1 MR56, MS120-8LP, MS250-24P, 16 MT) | must reproduce the measured live baseline |
| `BRANCH-RETAIL` | 750 nets × (2 MX + 1 MS24 + 3 MR) ≈ 4,500 dev | network-count-driven API budget |
| `CAMPUS` | 20 nets, ~4,000 MR + 1,200 MS48 ≈ 5,200 dev | dense wireless, per-AP fan-out |
| `DENSE-SWITCH` | 50 nets, 2,000 MS @ 48 ports ≈ 96k ports | cardinality / series explosion |
| `XL-MULTI-SITE` | 3,500 nets / ~20,000 dev | pagination depth, org ceiling |
| `MULTI-ORG-SHARD` | N instances × N orgs, one source IP | the 100 req/s per-IP limit (#700) |
| `CAMERA-HEAVY` | 30 nets × 800 MV | MV, the least-verified family |

Respect the vendor caps: 50,000 dev/org, 5,000 dev/network, MX 2, MG 4, MV 1,000, MT 1,700,
APs 5,000, switches 5,000 per network.

## Acceptance
- [x] Generator plus all seven presets committed
- [x] **`HOMELAB` reproduces the measured live values** — 4,677 series and 0.5341667 rps solved demand — within a stated tolerance. A preset that cannot reproduce the one shape we measured is not trustworthy for the six we cannot
- [x] **F-L9-08** — at least one test executes a genuine many-network collection: exact call counts, exact series counts, a 429 inside fan-out, a timeout, a partial failure, two overlapping runs, and metric expiry over churn
- [x] **F-L9-07** — CI tiering wired: PR runs `HOMELAB` + `BRANCH-RETAIL`; scheduled runs `CAMPUS`, `DENSE-SWITCH`, `XL-MULTI-SITE`; `MULTI-ORG-SHARD` and `CAMERA-HEAVY` on demand
- [x] **The `slow-tests` job's exit-5-as-success special case is removed** — zero collected tests must now be a failure
- [x] **`CAMERA-HEAVY`, and every absent-family element in any preset, is marked `SHAPE-ASSUMED`**, and the test output states which presets contained assumed shapes. A green run must never read as having verified a family nobody owns
- [x] Each preset emits a measured report: series count, RSS, calls per cycle, scrape render time and payload size
- [x] `make check` green

Parent: #694 · Closes finding **F-L5-05**

## Mechanism
The project mandates wrapping fetchers that may receive the SDK's exhausted-retry error shape with
`core.error_handling.validate_response_format`. An AST audit found **exactly four** direct response
fetches without it:

- `collectors/devices/ms_stack.py:73-118`
- `collectors/devices/mt.py:229-264` (the inventory-less fallback path)
- `collectors/organization.py:968-1036`
- `collectors/organization.py:1178-1235`

Each hand-rolls error-shape handling that returns empty or reclassifies an exhausted-retry or
rate-limit structure. The MS stack path can then **mark its endpoint group successful** on what was
actually a failure, which both delays retries and bypasses AIMD classification. Reachable by default
on the MS and organization paths.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L5-05** — all four call sites use `validate_response_format`
- [ ] No path can mark a group successful on an exhausted-retry response
- [ ] Tests feed the SDK's exhausted-retry dict shape to each of the four and assert the failure is classified, counted and retried
- [ ] A lint or AST check flags a future direct response fetch that skips the normaliser

Coordinator-level catches call `_track_error(UNKNOWN)` without preserving or classifying the original
exception: `collectors/devices/mt.py:175-204`, `collectors/network_health.py:592-610`,

comments.body:
## Live evidence: the status codes this exporter actually receives

Queried the m7kni Grafana stack on 2026-08-12 over a 14-day window of the <soak-host> soak's own
telemetry (`gcx --context m7kni metrics query -d grafanacloud-prom`):

```promql
count by (status_code) (max_over_time(meraki_exporter_api_requests_total[14d]))
```

| status_code | series |
|---|---|
| 200 | 108 |
| 503 | 11 |
| 502 | 3 |
| 404 | 1 |
| 530 | 1 |

Three things this settles, and they should drive the implementation rather than an assumed list:

1. **`530` is real.** That is a Cloudflare-origin status, not a documented Meraki API code. Whatever
   category table this issue lands must have a defined answer for it — and if today's classifier
   erases it into `unknown`, that is a concrete instance of this issue's defect rather than a
   hypothetical one. Check `530` explicitly.
2. **`502` and `503` dominate the non-200 population.** Transient upstream/gateway failures are the
   common real-world case, well ahead of anything endpoint-specific. They must not be erased into
   `unknown`, and they are genuinely retryable — distinct from the `404`/`402` case in #704.
3. **No `429` in 14 days.** Do not build or verify the category table on an assumption that 429s are
   routinely present in this deployment; they are not. 429 handling must still be correct, but its
   test evidence has to be synthetic or come from the #713 fault-injection harness.

Caveat on reading these numbers: this is a HOMELAB-shaped org (one network) and the counter resets
on every container restart, and the soak restarts on each push to `main`. Treat the table as
**which codes occur**, which is what this issue needs, and not as a rate or a total.

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D8** · Closes finding **F-L5-01** (a regression of #547)

## Mechanism
`core/org_health.py:149-207` — line 159 states in as many words that a failure in **ANY** domain backs
off the organization. Five failures engage org-wide backoff of 60–3,600 s.
`collectors/organization.py:644-686`, `collectors/device.py:675-714` and
`collectors/network_health.py:336-375` all consult that same shared tracker, skip work that would have
succeeded, and then raise `NothingCollectedError` once every org is skipped.

So **one license-gated optional endpoint returning 404 or 402 for five cycles withdraws every device,
network and organization metric for the whole estate.** A customer without an Insight licence loses
their switch metrics. Current logs independently reproduced a 429 → `unknown` → `NothingCollected`
cascade.

This is also the root of the alertability problem: a healthy 19-device org generated
`NothingCollectedError` 348 times on OrganizationCollector, 136 on DeviceCollector and 92 on
NetworkHealthCollector in 15 hours, which makes any alert on `collector_errors_total` unusable.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L5-01** — each domain or endpoint group tracks its own failure streak and backs off independently
- [ ] Org-wide suppression fires **only** on 401/403 on any call, or connectivity failure spanning multiple domains
- [ ] **404 and 402 never increment any streak** — "not licensed" is permanent state, not a failure, and should be recorded as such
- [ ] `NothingCollectedError` is raised only when it genuinely means nothing could be collected, and its counter is documented as alertable with a stated threshold
- [ ] Test: one permanently-404 optional endpoint leaves all other domains collecting normally
- [ ] Test: a 401 does suppress org-wide
- [ ] `make check` green

comments.body:
## Live evidence: a real 404 is observed in production

14 days of the <soak-host> soak's own telemetry, via the m7kni stack on 2026-08-12:

```promql
count by (status_code) (max_over_time(meraki_exporter_api_requests_total[14d]))
# 200:108  503:11  502:3  404:1  530:1
```

So the `404` this issue is about is not hypothetical — it occurs on a one-network homelab org. That
makes the premise sound and gives the fix a real target.

Two constraints for the implementation:

- **No `402` appears in the window.** A 402 (licence/entitlement) is the case most likely to appear
  on a customer org and least likely to appear here, so its handling cannot be verified from this
  deployment's telemetry. Prove it synthetically and say that is what you did.
- **Do not lump `502`/`503` in with `404`/`402`.** The gateway codes are transient and retryable; the
  404/402 case is "this endpoint is not available for this org, stop counting it against health".
  Conflating them would trade this bug for a worse one. See the companion note on #705.

Parent: #694 · Closes finding **F-L2-02** (a regression of #617 / #623)

## Mechanism
`collectors/clients.py:71-85` declares `CLIENTS_SIGNAL_QUALITY` with
`cost_fn = wireless_network_count × _SIGNAL_QUALITY_CLIENT_CAP`, and `_SIGNAL_QUALITY_CLIENT_CAP = 200`
(`clients.py:35`). `get_endpoint_groups` gates **only on `clients.enabled`** — so with
`clients.enabled=true` and the default `signal_quality_enabled=false`, the disabled group is still
registered and still contributes **phantom API cost** to the solver.

The docstring immediately above that method states the groups "must never enter the solver's demand
accounting" when disabled. The code checks the wrong flag.

Two further defects in the same area: disabled signal quality returns without marking success
(`clients.py:372-429` — only `clients_list` marks, at `:425-429`), and application usage uses only a
local timestamp. Never-successful groups stay permanently due, so the outer loop wakes at the **1 s
floor** (`core/scheduler.py:573-619`, `app.py:620-638`), which is the mechanism behind
`ClientsCollector` recording 108,790 histogram observations against `DeviceCollector`'s 1,560.

Phantom cost measured: `200 × wireless_networks / 600`. HOMELAB 0.333333 rps of the 0.5341667 rps
total — i.e. **most of the homelab's entire scheduled demand is for work that never runs**. At 500
wireless networks it is 166.67 rps floor, 41.67 at the cap.

This is live on <soak-host> right now, which runs `CLIENTS__ENABLED=true`.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L2-02** — child endpoint groups are registered and costed only when their own feature flag is enabled
- [x] Local-only successful work marks success, so no group stays permanently due
- [x] The outer loop no longer wakes at the 1 s floor with default client settings; assert the wake interval in a test
- [x] Solved demand for `clients.enabled=true, signal_quality_enabled=false` drops by the phantom term; assert the exact figure
- [x] `make check` green

Parent: #694 · Decisions: **D7**, and pairs with **D6** · Closes findings **F-L2-03**, **F-L5-02**

## Mechanism — F-L2-03
`core/scheduler.py:671-769` exposes solved interval, stretch, demand and budget, but **not**
`over_budget`, per-group last success, attempts, failures or skips. `/status` has point-in-time state
only, and a collector reporting success can mask a stale child group
(`core/collector.py:916-922`, `collectors/manager.py:814-854`). Live `/status` showed both client
child groups with `last_ran=null` while no metric existed to say so. Nothing is alertable.

## Mechanism — F-L5-02
`collectors/manager.py:419-455` `_collector_succeeded` only ever accumulates **first** successes;
readiness (`app.py:291-326`, `:975-990`) checks historical membership plus one prior HTTP 200. Failures
update a streak but never remove readiness, so `/ready` returns 200 forever once the exporter has
succeeded once — even after every collector has started failing. `/health` separately trips on
staleness.

**Do not "fix" this by making `/ready` freshness-based.** A NotReady pod is dropped from Service
endpoints, so Prometheus stops scraping and you lose the very metrics that explain the failure; and a
transient Meraki outage would stall or roll back deployments, turning a vendor problem into a
self-inflicted one. Per D7 the contract is documented and the signal moves to metrics.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L2-03** — bounded metrics for per-group last-success age, attempts, failures and skips
- [ ] A `scheduler` `over_budget` gauge exists and is alertable
- [ ] **F-L5-02** — `/ready` is explicitly documented as "initial collection completed" in the generated endpoint reference, `docs/deployment-operations.md` and the Helm chart's probe comments
- [ ] `/health` keeps the dead-man staleness check; the difference between the two is stated in one place
- [ ] Per-collector and per-endpoint-group last-success age is exported so alerting lives in Prometheus, not in a probe
- [ ] Example alert rules added under `grafana/alerts/` for staleness and over-budget
- [ ] Cardinality of the new metrics is bounded by group count, checked against the `XL-MULTI-SITE` preset
- [ ] `make docgen` + `make check` green

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D6** · Closes finding **F-L2-01**

Depends on the API facade (#698): the threshold is computed from demand, and until every call is
metered the demand figure is an estimate.

## Mechanism
`core/scheduler.py:233-334` and `:445-506` stretch each eligible endpoint group only to
`min(floor × 4, 3600)` and then **stop, even when demand still exceeds
`effective_budget × target_utilization`**. It merely logs `over_budget`. It also stretches
**priority 1 and 2** alongside everything else, so device availability degrades to 480 s and MT
sensor readings to 240 s while the plan remains unsustainable anyway.

For a monitoring product, stale up-ness is the worst possible thing to degrade — and it is being
degraded in service of a plan that does not come back under budget regardless.

Measured: HOMELAB solves to 0.5341667 rps and matches `/status` exactly. A modelled LARGE estate
gives 32.057778 rps floor demand and 9.0225 rps post-cap against a 5.6 rps target. The threshold is
crossed around 310 networks / 3,100 devices in that mix — but per D2 the mix itself was invented, so
the fixture presets must replace it.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L2-01** — the scheduler **stops stretching priority 1 and 2**; those keep their floors
- [ ] `collectors.profile` exists with `availability` (priority 1 only), `standard` (1–3) and `full` (everything)
- [ ] Above a threshold **computed from the solved plan versus budget** — not a raw network count, so it is shape-aware — startup **fails unless a profile is set explicitly**, naming the measured demand and the options
- [ ] Within a chosen profile, if demand still exceeds budget, priority 3/4 groups shed or defer rather than everything stretching
- [ ] Shed groups are named in a startup warning and visible in `/status`
- [ ] `docs/scaling-guide.md` and `docs/data-freshness.md` describe profiles and the shed policy
- [ ] Reproduce the threshold against the `BRANCH-RETAIL` and `CAMPUS` presets, not an assumed mix
- [ ] `make docgen` + `make check` green

body:
Parent: #694 · Decision: **D5** · Closes **N1** and **N2** — two findings the audit missed entirely, found during triage

## N1 — the 100 req/s per-source-IP limit is unknown to the product (HIGH)
Meraki enforces **two** limits, not one
(<https://developer.cisco.com/meraki/api-v1/rate-limit/>):

- **10 requests/second per organization**, shared across all applications using that org.
- **100 requests/second per source IP address**, shared by all clients using that IP.

`rg` over `src/` and `docs/` finds **zero** mentions of the per-IP limit — yet
`docs/scaling-guide.md` actively recommends sharding by organization. At the default 8 rps per shard,
**13 shards behind one NAT IP or one Kubernetes node exceed 100 rps** and every shard begins 429ing
simultaneously, with nothing in the product or the docs warning the operator. No audit lane checked
vendor limits beyond the per-org one.

Per **D5** this is documentation, not code: a single process cannot know how many siblings share its
egress IP, so enforcement would be guessing. Note this becomes load-bearing once the facade issue
disables SDK smart flow, which currently implements the per-IP cap as `SMART_FLOW_GLOBAL_RATE = 100`.

## N2 — verify `rate_limit_burst` against the documented allowance
`api.rate_limit_burst` defaults to **20** (`core/config_models.py:196`). Meraki documents the burst
allowance as **"an extra 10 requests in the first second"**, totalling **30 requests in two seconds**.
A 20-token bucket can emit 20 requests instantly at a cycle boundary, which appears to exceed the
documented +10 and would produce avoidable 429s every cycle. **Verify the bucket's actual semantics
against the documented shape before changing the default** — the two may not be directly comparable.

## Acceptance
- [x] **N1** — `docs/scaling-guide.md` documents both limits with the arithmetic
- [x] Recommended **shards per egress IP is capped (~8 at the default `shared_fraction`)**, with the alternatives stated: spread across egress IPs, or lower `shared_fraction`
- [x] The sharding recipe makes its egress-IP assumption explicit
- [x] The `MULTI-ORG-SHARD` fixture preset asserts the arithmetic
- [x] **N2** — a written comparison of the token bucket's behaviour against "+10 in the first second, 30 in two seconds", and either a corrected default or a recorded reason the current one is right
- [x] `make docgen` green

comments.body: Docs evidence complete in docs/scaling-guide.md: records the 100 req/s per-source-IP limit, the <=8 default-shards-per-egress-IP operational recommendation (64 req/s), NAT/egress assumptions, exact current network-health equivalents (4.58 and 1,041.3 calls/300 s), and the burst comparison. The limiter starts full; the former burst=20 + default 8 req/s permits 36 in two seconds, so the documented 30-in-two-seconds envelope requires the corrected conservative default 10. Root resume: retain the MULTI-ORG-SHARD fixture assertion and run the final docgen/check gate.

Parent: #694 · Closes findings **F-L6-02**, **F-L6-03**

## Mechanism — F-L6-02 (HIGH)
`collectors/organization_collectors/api_usage.py:107-134` calls `getOrganizationApiRequests` with
only `timespan=3600, total_pages="all"` and **no `perPage`**. The vendor default is **50** while the
maximum is **1,000**, and the SDK follows every `Link` header
(`meraki/session/sync.py:233-306`). The scheduler costs the whole group at **two calls**
(`collectors/organization.py:77-81`).

Measured on the homelab: `H = 2,841` rows/hour → `P = ceil(H/50) = 57` pages against an assumed cost
of 2. At a sustained 8 rps for an hour, `H = 28,800` → **576 pages**. At `perPage=1000` those become
3 and 29. So the telemetry that is supposed to explain an incident becomes a material or dominant
part of the budget during one, and the failure path is best-effort, so the operation breakdown
silently disappears exactly when it is needed. Partially covered by #274.

## Mechanism — F-L6-03 (MEDIUM)
`collectors/devices/ms.py:901-920` and `:1433-1474` pass an **unchunked list of every switch serial**
to two org-wide endpoints; the SDK encodes repeated `serials[]` parameters
(`meraki/api/switch.py:3375-3440`). `Q(S) = S`: 2 terms on the homelab, **5,000 terms and >75 KB of
encoded key material** at LARGE, risking a 414 or gateway rejection.

**The fix sidesteps the unverifiable question entirely.** Do not try to establish what URL length
Meraki accepts — omit the `serials` filter for an all-org fetch, since org scope and pagination
already bound the result. This is why this issue needs no large-fleet access.

## Acceptance
- [ ] **F-L6-02** — `perPage` is set to the endpoint's documented maximum (1,000) here and audited across every other paginated call
- [ ] The endpoint group's cost function reflects expected pages, not a flat 2
- [ ] A truncated or deadline-cut bulk fetch emits a completeness signal rather than reporting success — a silently truncated fetch is a wrong-data defect
- [ ] **F-L6-03** — the `serials` filter is omitted when fetching all org devices; if any call genuinely needs filtering, it chunks conservatively and reports completeness
- [ ] Tests assert the emitted query string for both paths
- [ ] `make check` green

body:
Parent: #694 · Decision: **D4** · Closes findings **F-L1-01**, **F-L1-02**, **F-L1-03**, **F-L6-01**, **F-L5-03**

The largest single change in the programme. Land it before P2's over-budget work — the profile
threshold is computed from demand, and until this lands nobody can measure actual wire rate.

## Mechanism
**Two limiters pace the same traffic and neither knows about the other.** `api/client.py:179-218`
passes `wait_on_rate_limit=False` but never sets `smart_flow_enabled`, and the pinned SDK defaults it
on (`meraki/config.py:90` `SMART_FLOW_ENABLED = True`) at its own 9 rps per-org bucket
(`config.py:95`), blocking worker threads before requests and making its own mapping-hydration calls.
`OrgRateLimiter` meanwhile paces at 8 rps (10 × `rate_limit_shared_fraction` 0.8).

Two further consequences of smart flow being on, both found during triage:
- `SMART_FLOW_GLOBAL_RATE = 100` (`config.py:100`) — the SDK is currently the **only** thing
  implementing the per-source-IP limit. Disabling it removes that; covered by documentation in
  the budget-truth issue, per D5.
- `SMART_FLOW_CACHE_PATH = ~/.meraki/.cache/rate_limit_cache.json` (`config.py:106`) with a 7-day TTL
  (`config.py:112`) — writes rate-limit state into `$HOME` and persists it across restarts, which
  fails or lands somewhere unintended on a read-only root filesystem.

**A third path bypasses both limiters.** `collectors/devices/mr/firewall.py:202` `_collect_ssid_rules`
is **undecorated**, and its per-SSID L3 and L7 fetches at `:223` and `:254` are raw
`asyncio.to_thread` calls — no `log_api_call`, no `OrgRateLimiter.acquire`, no retry owner. Worse, the
`@log_api_call("getNetworkWirelessSsidFirewallL3FirewallRules")` decorator sits on the **outer**
`collect_ssid_firewall` (`firewall.py:80`), so telemetry attributes a single call to an endpoint that
is really hit N times unmetered. Cost is `W + 2·E·W`; at `W=400, E=4` that is 3,600 GETs, 400–450 s,
well past the 240 s collector timeout.

**Nothing measures the real rate.** `meraki_exporter_api_requests_total` claims to count all exporter
calls but increments only in `OrganizationInventory._make_api_call` (`api/client.py:236-262`,
`services/inventory.py:244-302`). Direct collector calls, pagination, retries and SDK-generated
requests are all absent. And `inventory.py:256-300` awaits `to_thread` directly, outside
`with_error_handling` and `asyncio.timeout`, so cold cache refreshes have no deadline, no retry owner
and no AIMD classification (**F-L6-01**, a regression of #546).

Because the only org-wide request telemetry is Meraki's own trailing-hour **all-client** gauge, a
real exporter 400 cannot be attributed to an endpoint or caller (**F-L5-03**) — the audit had to use
the Dashboard request audit log to establish that 59 of the observed 400s were somebody else's
action-batch POSTs.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L1-01** — `smart_flow_enabled=False` passed explicitly; `OrgRateLimiter` is the sole pacer
- [x] **F-L1-02** — no raw `asyncio.to_thread` SDK call remains outside the facade. Measured scope: **141 call sites**
- [x] The misplaced `@log_api_call` on `collect_ssid_firewall` is corrected so endpoint attribution matches the calls actually made
- [x] **F-L1-03** — `meraki_exporter_api_requests_total` counts every attempt, page and retry, with endpoint and status labels; HELP text no longer over-claims
- [x] **F-L5-03** — an exporter-issued 400 is attributable to an endpoint from `/metrics` alone; the Meraki-sourced org metric is relabelled as aggregate all-client product data
- [x] **F-L6-01** — inventory fetches go through the facade and honour `per_fetch_deadline_seconds`, with an explicit stale-cache outcome on deadline
- [x] **An AST or lint gate fails CI on any new SDK call outside the facade** — without this a missed site silently reopens the bypass and nothing else would catch it
- [x] Verify no second 429-retry owner survives anywhere (SDK session layer, collectors, `api_helpers.py`)
- [x] `make check` green

Parent: #694 · Decision: **D1** · Closes finding **F-L8-01** (the audit's only BLOCKER)

## Mechanism
`server.api_token` defaults to `None` (`core/config_models.py:782`). `_check_api_token`
(`app.py:328`) then returns immediately — its own docstring states the control endpoints "stay open"
by design. Both mutating routes call it and proceed:

- `/api/collectors/trigger` (`app.py:1130`) → `run_collector_once(..., force=True)`, which bypasses
  every cadence gate (`collectors/manager.py:348`).
- `/api/clients/clear-dns-cache` (`app.py:1102`) → mutates DNS resolver state.

Separately, the running check is **non-atomic**: `manager.py:711` tests `collector_lock.locked()`
*before* awaiting `self._collector_semaphore`, so two forced tasks can both pass the check and queue.

Default bind is `0.0.0.0:9099`, so one network-reachable POST consumes the shared Meraki budget,
queues work and forces DNS re-resolution. Repeated POSTs amplify it.

This **overturns #558 / F-167**, which knowingly left POST authentication optional. That is
deliberate — see D1 on #694.

## Acceptance
- [x] **F-L8-01** — mutating POSTs return `401` when `server.api_token` is unset
- [x] No insecure opt-in flag is added (explicitly rejected in D1)
- [x] Web UI omits or disables the trigger and DNS-clear buttons, with an explanatory tooltip, when no token is configured
- [x] At most one pending-or-running forced task per collector, enforced atomically (fix the check-then-acquire race at `manager.py:711`)
